alternate_angle_derivation.step_2_consequence: A settling witness must therefore carry three things at once: (1) a fixed date, (2) an identified institution, (3) a material/find context. quoted_passages.text: 'House F' was in operation in Nippur during the 1740s BCE (the early reign of king Samsu-iluna). It was excavated by the joint Chicago-Philadelphia expedition in 1951-52, yielding nearly one and a half thousand fragments of tablets.

quoted_passages.text: The house consisted of a small courtyard, locus 192, with three small rooms (191, 189, and 184) ranged to its northwest and a larger back room or courtyard, 205, to its northeast.

quoted_passages.text: while most houses excavated in Area TA yielded at most a few handfuls of tablets totalling 209, House F produced 1, 425 fragments, over 85% of the entire number found in TA that season (Fig. 5; McCown and Haines 1967: pl. 160 D). And whereas the tablets in the other houses were a roughly equal mixture of administrative and legal documents, Sumerian literature, and elementary school tablets, in House F only 2% of the tablets are clearly archival in character. Over 50% contain Sumerian literature, 42% are other school documents, and 6% remain to be identified (Fig. 7).
quoted_passages.extraction_note: the space in '1, 425' reproduces the source rendering

quoted_passages.text: The established understanding of this situation is that the Old Babylonian scribal schools were deliberately traditionalist, continuing to promulgate Sumerian while most administrative, business, and legal documents were already written in Akkadian (e.g., Pearce 1995: 2270).

Some thirty or so household documents written after Hammurabi's conquest of Nippur in 1762 survive from House F and its neighbours in Area TA. Over two thirds of them were written in Sumerian (Fig. 15), and continued to be written in Sumerian until the area was abandoned after 1721 (Fig. 16).

settling_passages.why_this_settles: It is the scholarly passage the residual asked for, and it is object-anchored: a named house, a stated operation window (1740s BCE, abandoned after 1739 per paragraph 4), a quantified assemblage (1,425 fragments; 2% archival vs >50% Sumerian literature), and the explicit statement of the register separation (schools promulgating Sumerian while legal/administrative documents were Akkadian).

whole_claim_support.basis: All four legs of the entry's line-39 row and the entry's line-14 coupling criterion are now backed by (i) a peer-reviewed microstudy of the institution (Robson 2001), (ii) two open-access documents that state dated objects' findspots inside that institution (ISACMP 1; OIP 78), and (iii) the 2023 institutional statement that the school operated when Sumerian was no longer spoken.
whole_claim_support.qualification: Nothing retrieved states a single vernacular-loss date; the entry asserts none. No retrieved source claims that a text found in House F names the building as a school (see negative claims).

what_remains_unanswerable.limit: No retrieved text names House F as a school from inside the house itself; the identification is assemblage-statistical, and the 2023 catalogue hedges it ('widely believed to have been a scribal school', printed p. 3). Any claim that a specific dated tablet 'names the institution as a school' is therefore unanswerable from public sources — the institution is inferred from the find assemblage (Robson 2001 paragraph 5: 2% archival vs >50% Sumerian literature vs neighbouring houses' mixed profile).

Secure internal dates and secure find contexts trade off in this corpus, by the sources' own statements: school documents are 'rarely' internally dated (ISACMP 1 printed p. 9), while the primary publication warns that dated tablets in houses are 'unstratified' and that levels can be dated only approximately from tablets (OIP 78 printed p. 74). A maximally strong version of the question — 'a dated school text that also proves its own findspot' — is unanswerable by construction; what exists instead is (a) internally dated house documents with recorded findspots (the two catalog entries above, though both are house-sale/exchange documents rather than school exercises and both sit in the house's Level X phase) and (b) school exercises dated only by their context.

Level labels for House F are not uniform across the retrieved documents: the 2023 catalogue places the two dated documents at 'Level X Floor 1' (printed pp. 226-227) and the great school assemblage at 'Level XI' (printed p. 34), while OIP 78's contents list names 'TA House F (Level XI 1)/(XI 2)' as the representative house phases and OIP 78's dated-tablet table places 3NT 87 under a 'Level X 1' block. The exact phase in which the school operated versus the phase in which the two dated documents were deposited is therefore not fully pinned by the retrieved text; whether the Level X documents post-date the school's main phase (the 'post-school layer' mentioned in ISACMP 1) is left as to-verify.
evidence: OIP 78 printed p. 76 (Level X 1 block) vs printed p. xii (Level XI 1/2)

what_remains_unanswerable.limit: The tablet objects themselves were not inspected (no museum record retrieved; see access_failures), so object-level attributes (material, dimensions, seal impressions) are cited at second hand from the 2023 catalogue.
